newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Tax problems threaten next IMF Russia handout.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Tax problems threaten next IMF Russia handout.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund slammed on the brakes in its dealings with Russia on Tuesday and said payment of part of a $10 billion loan was not likely yet.
"The (IMF) mission is not yet in a position to recommend the release of the latest tranche," IMF Moscow representative Martin Gilman told Reuters.
A Finance Ministry official said the release of the tranche -- about $320 million -- would depend on how the IMF viewed Russia's January figures. But he admitted tax revenues were low.

"We have not fulfilled some demands of the IMF's monetary programme, including revenues," Finance Ministry macroeconomic department head Anton Siluanov told Reuters. "But we do not think this may be a reason for freezing the tranche."
The IMF approved the three-year loan last year, but monthly payments depend on Russia meeting tough targets on inflation, revenue and the budget deficit.

Inflation -- prices rose 19.7 percent in the year to January -- is within the promised range, but dismal tax collection has slowed much-needed social reforms and hurt sectors of the economy which once used state funds to survive.

A long delay in paying the loan will ring alarm bells in Russian financial markets, which viewed an IMF decision earlier this month to hand over two tranches worth almost $650 as a vote of confidence which helped drive share prices to record highs.

The IMF reviews the Russian economy each month to decide whether to release tranches of the loan and it delayed payments in the final quarter of last year, complaining Russia was not collecting enough tax to meet its budget plans.
But the Washington-based organisation relented earlier this month, paying two tranches and praising Russia for "several important structural reform measures".
Analysts said the latest delayed tranche would probably be paid soon.
"My own view is that they will get the money after the next round of talks," said one Western economist. "The IMF needs to assess January figures in the context of plans for the year."
Analysts said January's poor tax collection meant reforms could be losing steam again.

"The stability of the stabilisation programme remains in question because of difficulties on the fiscal side," said Charles Blitzer, chief economist, emerging markets at Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette in London.
"Structural reform is going to be a slow and painful process in Russia and that is what is keeping the economy from recovering."

The government has set up a special commission to force tax debtors to pay and officials are working on a new tax code. But tax evasion is rampant and many doubt whether the code will get through the communist-dominated lower house of parliament.
Russia's economic picture is, as ever, mixed.
Inflation is at its lowest level since economic reforms began in 1992 and industrial output and gross domestic product have stabilised after years of steep declines.
But the tax debts and a vicious cycle of non-payments affecting virtually every sector of the economy remain two of Russia's biggest economic problems.
Analysts also say the 1997 budget, approved by parliament earlier this month, contains unrealistic revenue forecasts -- 404.26 trillion roubles ($71.2 billion).
"The budget is politics," Siluanov said. "What we are talking about with the IMF is real life." ($ = 5675 Russian Roubles)
